slides.title: Rational Agents
slides.content: Rational Agents We’ll use the term rational in a very specific, technical way:  Rational: maximally achieving pre-defined goals  Rationality only concerns what decisions are made (not the thought process behind them)  Goals are expressed in terms of the utility of outcomes  Being rational means maximizing your expected utility Alternative title for this course would be: Computational Rationality or… Automated Intelligence

slides.title: What About the Brain?
slides.content: What About the Brain? Brains (human minds) are very good at making rational decisions, but not perfect Brains aren’t as modular as software, so hard to reverse engineer! “Brains are to intelligence as wings are to flight” We can’t build AI at the scale of the brain (~100T synapsis on a lunchbox) Still, the brain can be a great inspiration for AI!

slides.title: Designing Rational Agents
slides.content: Designing Rational Agents o An agent is an entity that perceives and acts. o A rational agent selects actions that maximize its (expected) utility. o Characteristics of the percepts, environment, and action space dictate techniques for selecting rational actions o This course is about: o General AI search techniques for a variety of problem types o Learning to recognize when and how a new problem can be solved with an existing technique Agent ? slides.title: Course construction at KU Leuven,
slides.content: Course construction at KU Leuven, an ECTS reminder 1 ECTS point corresponds to about 25-30 hours of study. Lectures: 3 ECTS points = 75-90 hours 11 lectures covering 20 hours -> 55-70 hours remaining let's say you will study 4 days of 8 hours for the exam = 32 hours -> still 23-38 hours of study expected to understand the material! Same for exercises: 1 ECTS = 25-30 hours expected; only 15 hours of guided sessions Project: 25-30 hours expected (remove/add based on programming experience)

slides.title: A (Short) History of AI
slides.content: A (Short) History of AI o 1940---1950: Early days, thinking meets computer science o 1943: McCulloch & Pitts: Boolean circuit model of brain o 1950: Turing's “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” o 1950—1970: Excitement! Logic-driven o 1950s: Early AI programs, including Samuel's checkers program, Newell & Simon's Logic Theorist, Gelernter's Geometry Engine o 1956: Dartmouth meeting: “Artificial Intelligence” adopted o 1965: Robinson's complete algorithm for logical reasoning

slides.title: Shakey the robot
slides.content: Shakey the robot (SRI International, 1966-1972) Computer Vision (Hough Transf) A* search STRIPS planning ... Declared IEEE Milestone https://ethw.org/Milestones:SHAKEY:_The_World%E2%80%99s_First_Mobile_Intelligent_Robot,_1972

slides.title: A (Short) History of AI
slides.content: A (Short) History of AI o 1970—1990: Knowledge-based approaches o 1969—79: Early development of knowledge-based systems o 1980—88: Expert systems industry booms o 1988—93: Expert systems industry busts: “AI Winter” o 1990—2000: Statistical approaches o Resurgence of probability, focus on uncertainty o General increase in technical depth o Agents and learning systems… “AI Spring”?

slides.title: o 2000—2022: Big data, data science and machine learning
slides.content: o 2000—2022: Big data, data science and machine learning o Big data, big compute o Data science as an overarching theme o Some re-unification of sub-fields o Task-specific AI used in many industries o 2022—: ChatGPT and Generative AI o Nov 22: ChatGPT with GPT3.5 unleashed o Neural networks with transformer architecture are everywhere o AI Research companies, e.g. DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, ... o Generative AI: Dall-E, Segment Anything, SeamlessM4T, ... o Public access: ChatGPT, Bing Search/Co-pilot, Gemini on Pixel9, ... A (Short) History of AI
